original_value: Effective network intrusion detection techniques are required to thwart evolving cybersecurity threats. Historically, traditional enterprise networks have been researched extensively in this regard. However, the cyber threat landscape has grown to include wireless networks. In this article, the authors present a novel model that can be trained on completely different feature sets and applied to two distinct intrusion detection applications: traditional enterprise networks and 802.11 wireless networks. This is the first method that demonstrates superior performance in both aforementioned applications. The model is based on a one-versus-all binary framework comprising multiple nested sub-ensembles. To provide good generalization ability, each sub-ensemble contains a collection of sub-learners, and only a portion of the sub-learners implement boosting. A class weight based on the sensitivity metric (true-positive rate), learned from the training data only, is assigned to the sub-ensembles of each class. The use of pruning to remove sub-learners that do not contribute to or have an adverse effect on overall system performance is investigated as well. The results demonstrate that the proposed system can achieve exceptional performance in applications to both traditional enterprise intrusion detection and 802.11 wireless intrusion detection.

result.paraphrase: Effective network intrusion detection methods are needed to counter evolving cybersecurity threats. Although traditional enterprise networks have long been studied in this area, the threat landscape now also encompasses wireless networks. In this article, the authors introduce a novel model that can be trained on entirely different feature sets and used for two separate intrusion detection tasks: traditional enterprise networks and 802.11 wireless networks. It is the first approach to show superior performance in both of these applications. The model uses a one-versus-all binary framework with multiple nested sub-ensembles. To promote strong generalization, each sub-ensemble includes a set of sub-learners, and only some of them use boosting. Each class’s sub-ensembles are assigned a class weight derived from the sensitivity metric (true-positive rate) and learned only from the training data. The study also examines pruning to eliminate sub-learners that do not help, or that hurt, overall system performance. Results show that the proposed system can deliver outstanding performance for both traditional enterprise intrusion detection and 802.11 wireless intrusion detection.
